title: Sharks
objective: After this level you can describe sharks and their senses.
summary: Sharks are boneless, cartilage-framed fish older than trees. NOAA counts eight senses, from a sharp nose to a lateral line that feels pressure changes. Bites are rare: 65 unprovoked worldwide in 2025.

cards.headline: Sharks are older than trees.
cards.body: Sharks have been around for about 400 million years. The earliest trees showed up around 350 million years ago. So sharks were cruising the seas before the first forest cast a shadow. What is an animal that old built from, and how does it find its food?

cards.headline: A skeleton you could bend
cards.body: Sharks are fish, but they have no bones at all. Remember Level 41's bony fish, with scales of bone? Sharks are the other kind: cartilaginous fishes. Their whole skeleton is cartilage, the lightweight, flexible stuff that shapes your ear. Fold your ear over and let go. That's shark skeleton material.

cards.headline: Eight senses
cards.body: NOAA counts eight shark senses. Five are ones you have too: sight, hearing, smell, touch and taste. A shark's nose is famously sharp; it can smell blood in the water from a long way off. Then there's the lateral line, a row of tiny pores running from snout to tail. As water flows through them, sensory cells pick up changes in pressure. A shark feels the water around it move.

cards.fact: Shark bites are rare: 65 unprovoked bites worldwide in 2025.
cards.context: That count comes from the International Shark Attack File, which tracks bites around the world. The 2025 total was in line with the average of 61 a year from 2020 to 2024, and the File calls the number extremely low. Eight senses tuned for finding food, 400 million years of practice, and people are still very rarely on the menu.
